rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands on the evidence. Its best angle, “Blood-oxygen tracking on Eight Sleep's smart bed is a top-subscription-tier feature, not a standard one,” is built from two supplied facts and asks for the exact proof a reporter would demand. B has better headline instincts, but “Your mattress now watches your blood oxygen. Doctors have questions.” buys drama with unsupplied medical and regulatory claims. That is not strategy; that is a lawsuit wearing a subject line.
gaps_in_A: “live clinical study with an unnamed sleep clinic” contradicts the update’s “named sleep clinic” framing; if the name exists, do not pretend it does not just to heighten the mystery.
“Beds are becoming health sensors, one mattress cover at a time” is a one-company trend until A finds other examples. It admits the proof gap, but the kept angle is still soft.
“an audience that already tracks HRV and sleep stages” imports behavior not supplied in the update. The athlete/biohacker angle needs a real user or customer proof before it leaves the building.
gaps_in_B: “low overnight blood oxygen is the primary marker of sleep apnea, which affects tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed” may be plausible, but it is not in the update. B smuggles in medical facts to make the angle hotter.
“Consumer SpO2 monitoring has been a live regulatory and clinical controversy since wrist-based devices added it” is an invented news peg. Useful if sourced, fatal if guessed.

“the funding and methodology haven't been disclosed” and “companies routinely commission studies designed to validate features rather than test them” turn absence of supplied detail into accusation. That is how you lose trust fast.
“On a $3,000 mattress” invents a precise price from “several thousand dollars.” Small number, big credibility problem.
